learningObjectives.title: The characteristic properties of acids and bases

questions.q: Which ion do all acids produce when dissolved in water?
questions.explain: Acids are substances that produce hydrogen ions (H⁺) in aqueous solution.

questions.q: In terms of proton transfer, a base is defined as a proton
questions.explain: In the 0620 syllabus a base is a proton (H⁺ ion) acceptor, while an acid is a proton donor.

questions.q: What is the correct definition of an alkali?
questions.explain: An alkali is a base that is soluble in water, producing hydroxide ions in solution.

questions.q: Which products are formed when a dilute acid reacts with a metal carbonate?
questions.explain: Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide, with the CO₂ seen as effervescence.

questions.q: What colour is methyl orange indicator in an acidic solution?
questions.explain: Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkaline (or neutral) solution.

questions.q: A solution turns litmus paper blue. What does this tell you about the solution?
questions.explain: Litmus turns blue in alkaline solutions and red in acidic solutions.

questions.q: Which pH value would you expect for a strong acid such as dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explain: Strong acids have low pH values (around 0-2); pH 7 is neutral and higher values are alkaline.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a strong acid and a weak acid of the same concentration?
options: A strong acid is fully ionised in solution, a weak acid is only partially ionised
A strong acid is more concentrated than a weak acid
A weak acid contains no hydrogen ions
A strong acid does not react with metals
questions.explain: Strong acids ionise completely in water, whereas weak acids only partially ionise.

questions.q: A student adds magnesium to dilute sulfuric acid and collects the gas produced. The gas gives a 'squeaky pop' with a lighted splint. What is the gas?
questions.explain: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen, and hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint.

questions.q: Non-metal oxides such as sulfur dioxide are generally classified as
questions.explain: Most non-metal oxides are acidic oxides that react with bases to form salts.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an amphoteric oxide?
questions.explain: Aluminium oxide (and zinc oxide) are amphoteric, reacting with both acids and bases.

questions.q: What is meant by an amphoteric oxide?
options: An oxide that reacts with both acids and bases to form salts
An oxide that reacts with neither acids nor bases
An oxide that only reacts with water
An oxide that produces hydrogen with metals
questions.explain: Amphoteric oxides, such as Al₂O₃ and ZnO, react with both acids and bases to form salts.

questions.q: Which oxide is a basic oxide?
questions.explain: Metal oxides such as copper(II) oxide are basic oxides that react with acids to form salts.

questions.q: Why does a basic oxide such as copper(II) oxide react with dilute sulfuric acid?
options: Because basic metal oxides neutralise acids to form a salt and water
Because it is an acidic oxide
Because it dissolves without any reaction
questions.explain: Basic oxides are the oxides of metals and neutralise acids to give a salt and water.

questions.q: A student wants to prepare pure, dry crystals of the insoluble salt lead(II) iodide. Which method should be used?
options: Precipitation by mixing two soluble salt solutions, then filtering
Titration of an acid with an alkali
Adding excess metal to an acid
questions.explain: Insoluble salts are made by precipitation, then filtered, washed and dried.

questions.q: When preparing a soluble salt from an acid and an excess of an insoluble base, why is excess base used?
options: To ensure all the acid has reacted, so the excess can be filtered off
To make the reaction produce hydrogen gas
To speed up evaporation of the water
questions.explain: Excess insoluble base guarantees all the acid reacts, and the leftover solid is simply filtered off.

questions.q: Using solubility rules, which of these salts is insoluble in water?
questions.explain: Most sulfates are soluble, but barium sulfate (like lead and calcium sulfate) is insoluble.

questions.q: Which statement about the solubility of salts is correct?
options: All sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble in water
All carbonates are soluble in water
All chlorides are insoluble in water
All nitrates are insoluble in water
questions.explain: All common sodium, potassium and ammonium salts, and all nitrates, are soluble in water.

questions.q: Which method is most suitable for preparing the soluble salt sodium chloride from sodium hydroxide solution and hydrochloric acid?
options: Titration using an indicator to find the exact volumes
Adding excess sodium metal to the acid
Filtering off an excess insoluble base
questions.explain: Because both reactants are soluble, titration is used to mix them in exact proportions before crystallising.

questions.q: What are the products of the reaction between an acid and a base?
options: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
questions.explain: The neutralisation of an acid by a base produces a salt and water only.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry (0620) syllabus; Acids, Bases & Salts
